quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Patrick would be ~25 in 1870 — possibly still in Thomas's household (Thomas ~52) or in his own nearby household. The collection 'United States Census, 1870' (1438024) is name-searchable. Patrick would be ~35 in 1880. Crucially, the 1880 census is the first to record each person's stated relationship to the head of household — if Patrick is enumerated in Thomas's household (Thomas ~62), the enumerator would record 'son,' which is stronger evidence than mere co-enumeration in earlier years. If Patrick has his own household by then, Thomas may appear as a boarder or parent, again with a stated relationship. The collection 'United States Census, 1880' (1417683) is name-searchable.

Patrick died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. Pennsylvania civil death registration began in 1906, so a state death certificate exists. S3 ('Pennsylvania Death Certificates') is already cited in the tree for Patrick's death fact, but no assertions naming his parents have been extracted from it for q_001. The informant (typically a family member) may have provided Patrick's father's name, mother's maiden name, and birthplace — all primary parentage evidence. The birth-parish discrepancy (tree records Ireland; objective says Pennsylvania) may also be resolved here.

A will filed by Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. The loc_001 locality entry notes that probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811 and are available via FamilySearch. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), so this requires an image browse of the county probate dockets rather than a name search. Thomas was born ~1818; his death is unknown but could plausibly fall anywhere from ~1858 to ~1910, so the item's date range is set to Thomas's plausible death window rather than Patrick's research window.

A dedicated search for the marriage record of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required for a parentage question. This record (a) confirms the couple as a unit; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which no census or the 1908 death certificate is likely to give; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845), corroborates that Thomas was the father of a child named on later derivative sources such as a death certificate or single co-residence. Note the limit: the marriage record alone does not prove Patrick is their child — it establishes the couple and dates their union. loc_001 notes that Roman Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia through this period; the collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. The mother's surname produced here should be treated as her surname at time of this marriage, which may be a prior married name rather than her birth name; a companion search for her earlier marriages or her own baptism may be needed if remarriage is suspected.

If Patrick was born in Schuylkill County (as the objective states, in contrast to Ireland in the tree), a Catholic baptism record would directly name his parents and constitute primary evidence of parentage. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. If the baptism cannot be found — because Patrick was born in Ireland as the tree records, or because the parish register predates surviving records — the absence shifts the search toward his death certificate (pli_008) and the 1880 census (pli_007) as the route to an origin, in keeping with loc_001's note that pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate rather than civil records.

FAN cluster item. If Thomas Flynn had other children, their baptism entries in Schuylkill County Catholic registers would each name Thomas and his wife as parents — directly confirming the family unit and identifying the mother. A sibling's baptism is stronger than co-enumeration alone because it places the same parental pair with a named child in a primary record. The collection 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Search for Flynn children baptized in the county across the range when Thomas (born ~1818) would have been raising a family; any match becomes a sibling lead and a corroborating parentage source for Patrick.

- **pli_004** — vital_record, Schuylkill County, 1908, FamilySearch: Patrick's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate; name-searchable; S3 is already in the tree on the relationship but no parentage assertions have been extracted — this is the highest-probability direct evidence source (death certs of this era name father and mother). - **pli_008** — census, Schuylkill County, 1900, FamilySearch: 1900 US Census (collection 1325221), name-searchable; lists month/year of birth, years married, and each person's parents' birthplaces — corroborates Ireland as Patrick's (and his parents') origin.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

If Patrick's wife is enumerated, her parents' birthplace columns may suggest the community ties that could help narrow an Irish parish of origin for a future search. A will or estate administration for Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence. Thomas was born approximately 1818 in Ireland; his plausible death range runs from the 1860s through the 1890s, the lifespan window of a man born around 1818 setting this item's date range to 1851–1900. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), requiring image browsing of Schuylkill County docket volumes. No wife is yet recorded for Thomas, so the estate may also reveal a mother's name among the heirs. A will naming Patrick as son or designating him as heir is direct evidence; an administration bond naming him next-of-kin is indirect corroborating evidence.

Marriage records in Pennsylvania frequently name the groom's parents and their birthplaces. Patrick would have married after reaching adulthood, likely between 1865 and his 1908 death. The Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950 (collection 1921317) is name-searchable; Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (collection 1571957) is also name-searchable and may cover earlier dates. For marriages in Schuylkill County before 1885, image group 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870–1910) is browse-only (personCount 0). Finding a marriage record that names Thomas and his wife as Patrick's parents would directly answer the question and reveal the mother's maiden name, which no existing source records. Try variant spellings Flyn and Flinn.

As a foreign-born Irish immigrant who was in Schuylkill County by 1850, Thomas Flynn would have needed to naturalize to become a U.S. citizen. Declarations of intent and petitions for naturalization made before the late 1870s often named the petitioner's wife and minor children, providing evidence of family composition that could directly name Patrick and his mother. Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0), requiring image-by-image browsing. Thomas's naturalization would likely fall between 1850 and 1875, based on his approximate age and arrival context. This is the FAN cluster item for this parentage question: finding Thomas's papers naming his wife and children, including Patrick, would corroborate the hypothesis and potentially supply the mother's name for the first time. The Flynn family was almost certainly Roman Catholic given their Irish origin in Schuylkill County's anthracite coal region. Baptismal registers name both parents of the child. A sibling of Patrick baptized in Schuylkill County would supply Thomas's wife's name and directly corroborate Thomas as a parent. The United States, Civil War Soldiers Index, 1861–1865 (collection 1910717) is name-searchable. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

Finding Michael in Schuylkill County as a miner in 1880 would show the move predated 1882; finding him still elsewhere as a farmer would narrow the migration window to 1880-1882. The 1870 Federal Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) corroborates and locates the starting point: the log records Michael as a farmer elsewhere in Pennsylvania in 1870. Finding this record would identify his specific pre-move county and township, confirm his occupation as farmer before the relocation, and establish a geographic anchor for the migration. Search surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan in Pennsylvania.

The 1900 Federal Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) would confirm Michael's continued presence as a miner in Schuylkill County roughly eighteen years after the stated relocation, strengthening the hypothesis that the coal industry was both the reason for and the anchor of the move. The 1900 schedule asked the year of immigration to the United States and the number of years in the country, which would provide important context if Michael was Irish-born, as the surname Sheahan strongly suggests.

Pennsylvania established the Bureau of Mines in 1870 and published annual Mine Inspection Reports naming individual collieries and their employees, including workers injured or killed in accidents. Finding Michael Sheahan's name in a report for a Schuylkill County colliery would be direct employment evidence linking him to anthracite coal-mining work in the county — the most specific documentation the question could have. The annual reports are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg and portions are available through Pennsylvania's digital collections. This occupation-specific record type falls under BCG Standard 14's topical breadth requirement.

The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, name-searchable) contains sacramental registers from coal-region parishes. The surname Sheahan is of Irish origin, suggesting Michael likely worshipped in a Catholic parish under the Diocese of Philadelphia (archdiocese from 1875, per loc_001). A baptism, marriage, or burial record placing him in a Schuylkill County parish in the early 1880s would narrow the migration date; some registers note the previous parish of origin, which could reveal where in Pennsylvania Michael lived before the move. The locality entry (loc_001) notes that the Diocese of Allentown was not erected until 1961, so records for this period fall under Philadelphia.

The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records (image group 007936750, 1849-1915) are browse-only (personCount 0) and must be examined image by image. If Michael immigrated from Ireland, his declaration of intention or petition for naturalization filed in Schuylkill County would record his stated occupation and residence. A filing in Schuylkill County rather than elsewhere in Pennsylvania would indicate he was already resident there at the time, corroborating the relocation. The locality entry (loc_001) confirms some naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups.

The Miners' Journal, published in Pottsville, Schuylkill County, is the principal newspaper of the anthracite coal region. It reported mine accidents, labor disputes (including actions of the Workingmen's Benevolent Association and later the United Mine Workers), colliery employment news, and community announcements. Finding Michael Sheahan's name in an accident report, labor-organization filing, or employment notice would directly document his coal-mining work and may identify the specific mine. Chronicling America (loc.gov) provides free, full-text-searchable access to digitized issues of the Miners' Journal for portions of this period.

The 1860 Federal Census (collection 1473181, name-searchable) is a fallback for the 1870 search (sequence 2). If the 1870 census does not yield a usable record, the 1860 census would extend the baseline further back and may locate Michael in Pennsylvania before his farming years, establishing a longer pre-mining trajectory. Search surname variants Sheahan, Sheehan, and Shehan in Pennsylvania.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) would be ~25 in 1870 — an adult, likely forming his own household or boarding. The United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Though the 1870 schedule does not record each person's relationship to the head of household (that column was not introduced until 1880), finding Thomas Flynn (born ~1818, now ~52) enumerated in the same household as Patrick would add a third decade of co-residence evidence to the two already established in 1850 and 1860, further strengthening the parentage inference. The search should also try variant spellings such as Flyn and Flinn.

If Thomas Flynn does not appear in Patrick's 1870 household, search for Thomas Flynn directly in Schuylkill County. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~52 and plausibly still alive and resident in the county. Finding Thomas in his own household — particularly with other members sharing the Flynn surname — would provide context for the family's composition after Patrick reached adulthood, and any member named Patrick would be direct corroboration of the relationship.

The 1880 census is the most probative of the three for this question because it was the first federal census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Patrick (~35) is old enough to be a household head; if Thomas Flynn appears in Patrick's 1880 household listed as 'Father,' that is direct parentage evidence on an original government record — far stronger than the inferred co-residence evidence from 1850 and 1860. Thomas (born ~1818) would be ~62 in 1880 and plausibly still alive. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable.

If Thomas is not in Patrick's 1880 household, search for Thomas Flynn directly. The 1880 relationship column in his own household would list any children still at home, and a Patrick Flynn listed as 'Son' to Thomas would constitute direct parentage evidence. The 1880 schedule also records each person's birthplace and their parents' birthplaces, which could confirm the family's Irish origin and further corroborate the parentage conclusion.

Patrick Flynn (d. 1908) will appear in the 1900 census at approximately age 55. The 1900 schedule is uniquely valuable because it asks for each person's parents' birthplaces, which could confirm Thomas Flynn's origin in Ireland — corroborating the parentage conclusion independently of the 1908 death certificate's secondary informant. The 1900 schedule also records years in the United States and citizenship status, which may help date the family's immigration. The United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Note: the 1890 census was largely destroyed by fire in 1921 and cannot fill the gap between 1880 and 1900.

The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father but was reported by a secondary informant (son-in-law James Brown). Finding Thomas Flynn's will naming Patrick as a son would provide direct parentage evidence on an original legal document and would advance the conclusion from 'probable' to 'proved.' The date range 1861-1900 covers Thomas's plausible death years: he was confirmed alive in 1860 and born ~1818, so he plausibly died between 1861 and roughly 1900 (at ~82); the census items above may help narrow this window. The loc_001 locality entry confirms Schuylkill County probate records (wills and administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills and are available from 1811. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) on FamilySearch is browse-only (personCount 0) — search by browsing the Schuylkill County volume by year rather than by name.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (already cited in the project tree as S3 for his death date and place) has not yet been reviewed for parentage information for q_001. Pennsylvania civil registration began in 1906 (per loc_001), so a 1908 death has a state certificate. The informant provided the deceased's parents' names and birthplaces as secondary information; if the informant was a family member who knew the parents, this is the fastest route to naming Patrick's mother and confirming or refuting Thomas Flynn as father. This is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Search with variant spellings Flinn and Flyn.

The 1860 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1473181, name-searchable) would show Patrick at approximately age 15. Finding him in Thomas Flynn's household a second time—a decade after the 1850 co-enumeration (a_004)—extends the indirect co-residence evidence for the Thomas-as-father hypothesis. The project tree cites this census as S2 on the parent-child relationship, but no parentage assertions have been extracted for q_001; this search anchors those assertions directly to the parentage question. Search for both Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County, with variant spellings Flinn and Flyn.

Thomas Flynn (born ca. 1818 in Ireland) plausibly died between 1851 and ca. 1900. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994 (FamilySearch collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0), as is the Schuylkill County probate image group 007936749 (1851–1930); browse both for a Thomas Flynn will or administration. A will explicitly naming Patrick as a son is direct evidence of parentage—the strongest available source short of a baptism record. The loc_001 entry confirms the Register of Wills has held Schuylkill County probate records since 1811. The date range is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan as a father of a child born ca. 1845, not by Patrick's own research window.

If the FamilySearch digital images (pli_006) do not yield a Thomas Flynn probate file, contact the Schuylkill County Register of Wills directly for a docket search covering 1851–1900. The loc_001 entry identifies this office as the custodian of the original records. Docket books list all filings by surname and name the heirs, so a Thomas Flynn entry naming Patrick as heir would constitute direct evidence of parentage even without the full will.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn and his wife is required by the parentage question. Their marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name—which no census or death certificate typically carries—and by its date relative to Patrick's birth (ca. 1845) corroborates Thomas as the father even when no record yet explicitly places Patrick as their son. Note the limit: the couple's marriage proves they married and dates their union but does not by itself establish Patrick as their child. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708–1985) is name-searchable. The Flynn family was likely Roman Catholic; Schuylkill County's RC parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia (per loc_001), and sacramental registers were held at the parish level. Thomas born ca. 1818 would have married roughly 1838–1855; the 1842 lower bound reflects when Schuylkill County church records first appear in this collection. If the marriage occurred in Ireland before immigration, no record may appear here and the browse-only fallback (pli_009) should be attempted.

If the name-searchable church collection (pli_008) returns no Thomas Flynn marriage, browse the Schuylkill County Church Records image group 007936751 (1842–1895), which is browse-only (personCount 0). The loc_001 entry notes that some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. Focus on Roman Catholic parishes in the coal-region communities where Irish immigrant families concentrated. This browse may also surface baptisms or burials for other Flynn family members that name Thomas's wife.

The 1870 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1438024, name-searchable) would show Patrick at approximately age 25 and Thomas at approximately age 52. By 1870 Patrick may head his own household or may still live with Thomas. Searching both names tracks the evolving household structure and extends the co-residence chain from 1850 and 1860. If Thomas's household in 1870 names a wife, her given name becomes a lead for the marriage search (pli_008). An Ancestry version of this census (external collection ancestry:7163) is a paid fallback if FamilySearch returns no results.

The 1880 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1417683, name-searchable) records each person's relationship to the head of household explicitly. If Patrick appears in Thomas Flynn's 1880 household listed as 'son,' that is a direct informant statement of parentage—still secondary evidence (the informant may be Thomas or his wife, not Patrick), but substantially stronger than the 1850 inferred co-residence (a_004). If Patrick heads his own household, the census records his parents' birthplaces (father's birthplace and mother's birthplace columns), which could confirm Ireland and potentially narrow a county. Patrick would be approximately age 35 and Thomas approximately age 62.

Patrick's own marriage record(s), if he married in Schuylkill County, may name his parents as witnesses or in the register entry—direct parentage evidence when the record identifies the groom's father and mother. The Schuylkill County Marriage Records image group (007936753, 1870–1910) is browse-only (personCount 0); the name-searchable church collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) also covers marriage registers for this period. Patrick would have married approximately 1865–1895 (ages 20–50). This item fulfills the FAN-cluster requirement for a parentage question: marriage witnesses were frequently siblings or other close relatives of the groom, and their names would expand the network available for follow-up. What this reveals about Patrick: a marriage entry naming Thomas Flynn or his wife as Patrick's parents is direct parentage evidence; a witness who is Patrick's sibling independently corroborates the same parentage.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization petition or declaration of intent, filed ca. 1849–1870 at the Schuylkill County court, would name his wife and potentially his minor children. Irish immigrants in the anthracite coal region naturalized at the county court; petitions from the 1850s–1860s often listed the petitioner's family by name. The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records image group (007936750, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). If Thomas's petition names Patrick as a son, that is direct parentage evidence. The date range is set by Thomas's plausible naturalization window, estimated from his birth ca. 1818 and his presence in Schuylkill County by 1850.

The 1900 US Census (FamilySearch collection 1325221, name-searchable) would show Patrick at approximately age 55 (he died in March 1908, so he is alive at the June 1900 enumeration). The 1900 census records parents' birthplaces (father's birthplace and mother's birthplace columns) for each person. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

This is a pedigree gap directly within the project objective. No plan has yet been written for this question.

entry.rationale: The United States Census 1880 (name-searchable) is the highest-probability single record for identifying children of Bridget and John Doyle. Children born 1858-1880 would be at peak household residency (ages 2-22). The schedule records each member's name, age, relationship to head, and birthplace; parents' birthplaces corroborate the Irish origin and distinguish this Doyle family from others in the county. Search surname Doyle in Schuylkill County, including spelling variants (Doyel, O'Doyle).

The United States Census 1870 (name-searchable) captures a mid-period snapshot of the Doyle household; children born by 1870 would be present. Cross-referencing the 1870 and 1880 returns helps triangulate birth years for each child and identify any who died between enumerations — an important step given that seven of nine children died before 1900.

The United States Census 1860 (name-searchable) is the earliest plannable federal census for this family. Bridget (born ~1838) and John Doyle's first one or two children may appear here. This record establishes the household anchor in Schuylkill County and corroborates the county of residence for all subsequent searches.

The 1900 census entry (log_002) already locates Bridget and confirms she had 9 children with 2 living. This search targets adult Doyle children who had established separate households in Schuylkill County by 1900. The United States Census 1900 (name-searchable) includes month and year of birth, valuable for reconstructing birth records for children whose baptisms may be unindexed. Also search neighboring households (FAN) for adult Doyle children still living nearby.

The United States Census 1910 (name-searchable) captures the two surviving Doyle children (confirmed living in 1900) ten years on. Cross-reference with 1900 results for continuity. Daughters who married will appear under their married names; use 1900 neighbors and known associates as FAN leads to track them into 1910.

Pennsylvania civil birth registration did not begin until 1906 (locality guide); baptism entries are the primary pre-1906 birth record and capture all children, including the seven who died before 1900. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) covers Catholic and Protestant parish registers. The Irish coal-mining community was predominantly Catholic under the Diocese of Philadelphia; search under Doyle with parents John and Bridget (also Halloran as the mother's surname). Burial entries in the same collection identify children who died young.

Image group 007936751 (browse-only, personCount 0) covers Schuylkill County church records 1842-1895, including parish registers not fully captured in the indexed collection. The locality guide notes some church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups. Browse volume by volume for Doyle family baptism and burial entries in the registers of the parish(es) the family attended.

Doyle daughters would appear under their maiden name before marriage. Image group 007936753 (browse-only, personCount 0) covers Schuylkill County marriage records 1870-1910 — the likely marriage window for children born 1858-1890. Marriage entries may also name the bride's parents, directly confirming parentage, and witnesses are frequently siblings or other close family members.

John Doyle appears to have died before 1900 — he is absent from Bridget's 1900 census household (log_002). His will or administration file would name surviving children as heirs. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 (browse-only, personCount 0) and Schuylkill County probate image group 007936749 (1851-1930, browse-only) are both available on FamilySearch. The Schuylkill County Register of Wills has held these records from 1811 (locality guide). The date range 1860-1900 is bounded by John Doyle's plausible death window, not the subject children's research window.

Seven of Bridget and John Doyle's nine children died before 1900. Grave markers and sexton registers in Schuylkill County's Irish Catholic cemeteries may identify these children by name, birth year, and death year. Search FindAGrave for the Doyle surname in Schuylkill County, particularly in cemeteries serving the Irish Catholic community. The two children living in 1900 may have died after Pennsylvania began civil death registration in 1906; once they are identified, check Pennsylvania death certificates (1906+) through the Pennsylvania State Archives.

- **pli_001** — church, Stagstrup Sogn, FamilySearch, 1778–1780: Indexed name search in Denmark Church Books (2078555, name-searchable); Stagstrup is 3% indexed so a hit is unlikely but the check costs little.

- **pli_003** — military, Thisted Amt, FamilySearch, 1789–1813: Indexed name search in Denmark Military Levying Rolls (2513529, name-searchable); levy rolls are direct parentage evidence — Mikkel appears under his father's name from ~age 10; rolls also note the father's death/departure.
- **pli_004** — military, Thisted Amt, FamilySearch, 1789–1814: Browse image group 004748896 (browse-only) for Stagstrup district entries. Fallback for pli_003.
- **pli_005** — census, Stagstrup Sogn, FamilySearch, 1787–1801: Name search in Denmark Census 1787–1930 (1401625); 1787 census shows Mikkel (~age 8) with parents and older siblings; 1801 census (age ~22) confirms whether father is still alive.
- **pli_006** — church, Stagstrup Sogn, FamilySearch, 1760–1779: Browse image group 004130616 for Niels's marriage to the mother, 1760–1778; confirms the couple and supplies the mother's maiden name.
- **pli_007** — church, Stagstrup Sogn, FamilySearch, 1760–1795 (FAN): Browse image group 004130616 for all baptisms listing Niels at Blyeberg as father; sibling entries corroborate the parental unit and may reveal the grandfather's name via naming patterns.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.question: Where did Josiah Rowe (b. ~1828, Ohio) reside between 1850 and 1865, and with whom was he living?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree places Josiah in Vigo County, Indiana at his death in 1879 and gives Ohio as his birthplace, but nothing is documented between his birth and his 1862 enlistment. No records have been searched yet.

entry.rationale: Josiah was born ~1828 in Ohio and at age ~22 in 1850 may still have been in Ohio or already in Indiana. The 1850 federal census lists every household member by name, age, and birthplace — directly answering where he resided and with whom. loc_001 notes that the census names every member but states no relationships, so all co-residents of his household must be recorded. loc_001 cites collection 1401638 (United States Census, 1850); personCount not confirmed by tool — treat as name-searchable. Search Rowe and variants Row and Roe across Ohio and Indiana.

Josiah enlisted in Indiana in 1862, strongly placing him in Indiana by 1860. The 1860 census lists every household member. loc_001 notes the census names members but not relationships, so full household enumeration must be recorded. loc_001 cites collection 1473181 (United States Census, 1860); personCount not confirmed by tool — treat as name-searchable. Focus on Vigo County but search all Indiana; also run Ohio as a check. Variants Row and Roe.

His 1862 Indiana enlistment record (Civil War compiled service record) names his place of enrollment and sometimes records pre-war residence. Muster rolls list fellow enlistees — often neighbors — identifying the community he came from and directly naming associates. Fold3 holds digitized NARA compiled service records for Indiana Civil War units; also check NARA directly for the originals if the index is incomplete.

loc_001 cites collection 1888129 (United States Civil War and Later Pension Files, 1861-1934). Pension depositions routinely include sworn statements of pre-enlistment residence, the names of neighbors who attest to identity, and family members sharing the household — primary evidence for the 1850-1862 residence gap. Date range extends to 1934 because a widow's or dependent's claim filed decades later can include affidavits covering events before 1865.

loc_001 notes that Vigo County tax and land records exist but are not indexed in any online collection; plan from the Indiana State Archives and the Vigo County Recorder. Annual tax lists name property holders by township, establishing when Josiah first appears in the county and filling the gap between census years. Deed books may name grantors and adjoining landowners (FAN). Window opens to 1845 to catch an early arrival before 1850.

FAN item. Search for other Rowe (Row, Roe) households in Ohio counties that supplied migrants to Vigo County, and in Vigo and adjacent Indiana counties. At ~22-32 Josiah most likely lived with or near a parent, brother, or cousin sharing Ohio birth origins; identifying them directly answers the cohabitation question. Also extract names of witnesses, neighbors, and bondsmen from any results returned by items 3-4 and search them here.

Ancestry's 1850 census index uses different name-variant logic than FamilySearch and may surface Josiah under Row or Roe where item 1 did not. Search if item 1 (FamilySearch 1850 Census) yields no result.
Ancestry's 1860 census index as a fallback if item 2 (FamilySearch 1860 Census) finds nothing. Different indexing and name-correction logic may catch variant spellings or OCR errors.
